digest.top_line: EBCTCG (62,923 women, ER+): after stopping endocrine therapy at 5y, distant recurrence in years 5-20 runs 13% (T1N0) to 41% (T2N4-9), at a steady annual rate.
digest.tldr: EBCTCG IPD: ER+ recurrence persists 15 years past endocrine therapy, scaled by T and N. RT read: MSKCC T1-2N1 without PMRT, 10y LRR 7.0% but 28% with age <40 + LVI; NSABP node-positive oLRR mortality HR 5.85; SAKK 23/82 tamoxifen after excision + RT for ILRR, 5-yr DFS 61% vs 40%, OS unchanged.

sites.intro: Five datasets on late and locoregional risk after mastectomy or lumpectomy + WBI. Four are prognostic or retrospective and one is randomized (SAKK 23/82). All feed PMRT and regional nodal RT selection.

studies.name: EBCTCG 20-year recurrence after 5 years of endocrine therapy
studies.tldr: After stopping endocrine therapy at 5y, distant recurrence in years 5-20 ran from 13% (T1N0) to 41% (T2N4–9), at a steady annual rate.
details: 🔍 EBCTCG IPD meta-analysis: 88 trials, 62,923 women with ER+ disease, disease-free at 5y of scheduled endocrine therapy
🔍 T1-T2, 0-9 positive nodes, diagnosed before age 75; Kaplan-Meier + Cox stratified by trial and treatment

details.text: 📊 Distant recurrence, years 5 to 20, by TN status
📊 T1N0 only, years 5 to 20, by tumor grade
📊 20-yr risk from year 0 (74,194 women, 78 trials), by nodal status

details: 📊 Contralateral BC ~0.3%/yr after stopping, independent of age or TN status
📊 Locoregional recurrence tracked the same risk factors as distant recurrence

details.text: 🔍 Other prognostic factors after year 5, given TN status
subdetails: Grade and Ki-67: strong in years 0-5, only moderate thereafter
PR status: prognostic years 0-5, not thereafter
HER2+ without trastuzumab: worse years 0-5, not thereafter

details: ⚠️ ~50% diagnosed before 2000 (range 1976 to 2011); no gene-expression profiles available
⚠️ Risks are for women SCHEDULED for 5y, not those who completed it; adherence largely unrecorded
⚠️ Authors estimate 5 to 10% of distant recurrences missed in trial records

verdict.rationale: Large multi-trial IPD prognostic analysis, not a randomised test of extension. Quantifies baseline late risk; extended-therapy benefit must come from separate randomised trials.
verdict.audience: ER+ T1-T2, 0-9 nodes, disease-free after 5y adjuvant endocrine therapy

studies.monday_clinic: In ER+ T1-T2 early breast cancer disease-free at 5 years, this frames the extension discussion around TN status, with T1N0 still carrying 13% distant risk over years 5 to 20; it does not address genomic-assay-selected or trastuzumab-treated HER2+ pts.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: EBCTCG **individual patient data meta-analysis** of 88 trials. Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression, stratified by trial and treatment, from year 5 to year 20.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **62,923 women with ER-positive T1-T2 disease, 0-9 positive nodes**, diagnosed before age 75, scheduled to stop endocrine therapy at 5 years and event-free at year 5. 63% tamoxifen, 17% AI, 20% a tamoxifen-AI sequence; all had lymph-node dissection.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Distant recurrence**, any breast-cancer event (distant, locoregional, contralateral), and death from breast cancer by log-rank subtraction.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Recurrences continued at a **steady rate from year 5 to 20** in every TN category. Given TN status, grade and Ki-67 carried only moderate independent value after year 5; PR and HER2 status were not predictive.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The source restates EBCTCG data that 5y tamoxifen cut recurrence by about 30% in years 5-10 versus no therapy. Extension trials such as ATLAS and MA.17 test the intervention; this analysis supplies the untreated baseline risk that their proportional benefit acts on.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents ER+ T1-T2, N0 to N4–9 pts who are disease-free after 5 years of adjuvant endocrine therapy. Does not represent pts with ≥10 nodes, tumors >5.0 cm, age ≥75, or genomic-assay-selected low-risk disease.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Grade and Ki-67 were often locally assessed, and Ki-67 was available in only 7692 pts. Few pts received trastuzumab (2%), and treatment eras predate modern staging and systemic therapy.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: No TN subgroup had a late risk low enough to dismiss extension outright, even **low-grade T1N0 at 10% distant recurrence**. Whether extension actually lowers mortality, and in whom it outweighs toxicity, is left to randomised data.

studies.interpretation:
The usable output of this analysis is a baseline, not a treatment effect. Extended endocrine therapy trials report proportional reductions, and the authors argue those reductions look roughly similar across risk groups, so the absolute gain from continuing past 5 years depends almost entirely on what a given woman's risk would be if she stopped. This paper supplies that denominator at a scale and follow-up no single trial can match: 62,923 women across 88 trials, followed to year 20. The headline finding is that the risk curve does not flatten. In every tumor-node category, distant recurrences kept accruing at a near-constant annual rate through the second decade, so the clinical intuition that ER+ disease that survives 5 years without event is largely cured does not hold.

The second finding is that anatomy outranks biology once the first 5 years have passed. Tumor size and especially nodal status remained powerful determinants of late distant recurrence, and their effects were roughly additive, running from 13% for T1N0 to 41% for T2N4–9. Grade and Ki-67, which carry strong prognostic weight early, lost most of their independent value after year 5, and PR and HER2 status lost theirs entirely. That pattern argues against using early-recurrence proliferation markers to talk a woman out of extension; the original TN stage remains the better guide. Even low-grade T1N0 disease carried 10% distant recurrence and 17% any breast-cancer event over years 5 to 20, which is the number that undercuts any claim of a group too low-risk to discuss.

Several design features should shape how confidently a reader applies these figures. The analysis is prognostic, drawn from within randomised trials but not testing extension itself, so it says nothing directly about how much continuing therapy would help. The cohort is old: about half were diagnosed before 2000, and better staging, surgery, radiation and systemic therapy since then likely shift absolute risks downward. Two biases pull in opposite directions. Risks were measured in women scheduled for 5 years regardless of adherence, so women who actually completed therapy probably did somewhat better, while the authors estimate that 5 to 10% of distant recurrences went unrecorded, so true rates are probably higher. HER2+ disease was largely untreated with trastuzumab, and no gene-expression data were available, which is the most important gap for current practice, where multigene assays already sort node-negative ER+ disease.

The decision this informs is the 5-year conversation in a disease-free woman. For node-positive or T2 disease, a steady late risk in the 20 to 40% range makes the absolute benefit of extension large enough to weigh seriously against toxicity. For T1N0, the risk is lower but not negligible, and the authors note that for women in reasonable health the competing risk of other-cause death will not erase it. What the paper does not settle is whether a genomic low-risk signature identifies a subgroup whose late risk truly falls below the threshold for benefit, and whether extension changes breast-cancer mortality rather than recurrence alone. For the radiation oncologist, the read is indirect: locoregional recurrence followed the same TN dependence as distant recurrence, so late locoregional events in the second decade are expected, not anomalous, in higher-stage ER+ disease.

significance_by_specialty.medonc: TN status, not grade or Ki-67, carries late-risk prediction after year 5, so the extension discussion should anchor on original stage. Even low-grade T1N0 retains 10% distant recurrence through year 20, leaving no clearly negligible-risk group without genomic data.

open_questions: Does a genomic low-risk score identify pts safe to stop at 5 years?
Does extended endocrine therapy reduce breast-cancer mortality, not just recurrence?
How much do modern-era treatments lower these late risks?

studies.name: SAKK 23/82
studies.tldr: 5-yr DFS 61% vs 40% with tamoxifen after excision + RT for good-risk post-mastectomy ILRR; OS unchanged (median 11.5 vs 11.2 yr, P=0.79).
details: 🔍 Phase III randomized, 178 randomized, 167 eligible 'good risk' women with ILRR after mastectomy
🔍 Good risk: ER+ recurrence, or ER unknown with DFI >12 mo and <4 nodules ≤3 cm
🔍 Local therapy both arms: radical excision, then 5000 cGy at 200 cGy/fx to the involved region
💊 Randomized to tamoxifen 20 mg/d until progression vs observation; prior adjuvant TAM excluded
🔍 Stratified by menopausal status, adjuvant chemo, axillary nodes at diagnosis. Median f/u 11.6 yr in survivors
📊 Per authors, further LOCAL recurrence was the only failure type TAM reduced on cumulative incidence analysis
⚠️ Log-rank DFS P=0.053; nominal significance rests on the early-weighted Gehan-Wilcoxon test
⚠️ Premenopausal subgroup only n=35; the OS signal against TAM is underpowered
⚠️ Accrual 1982-1991; most current ILRR pts have already had adjuvant TAM and would not have been eligible

verdict.rationale: Mature phase III, but small, 1980s accrual, borderline log-rank DFS and no OS gain. Backs current endocrine therapy after resected ILRR without defining it for TAM-pretreated pts.
verdict.audience: Good-risk ILRR after mastectomy, post excision + RT, TAM-naive

studies.significance: For the RT reader, failure after excision plus 5000 cGy at 200 cGy/fx was mostly further local recurrence, and TAM mainly reduced that, not distant spread. Endocrine therapy works here as a local-control partner to chest wall RT. ILRR is also not always a metastatic marker: about 30% stayed relapse-free on local therapy alone.
studies.monday_clinic: In a postmenopausal woman with ER+ isolated chest wall or nodal recurrence after mastectomy, resected and irradiated, this supports adding endocrine therapy for DFS. It does not cover premenopausal pts, who gained no DFS, or pts who already had adjuvant TAM.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Phase III randomized**, central telephone randomization at SAKK, stratified by menopausal status, adjuvant chemo and axillary nodes at diagnosis. 178 randomized, 11 ineligible (6%). **Median f/u 11.6 yr** for surviving pts.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Good-risk ILRR after mastectomy**: first recurrence in the ipsilateral chest wall, shoulder, neck or upper arm, or in regional nodes. Eligibility required an **ER+ recurrence**, or ER unknown with **DFI >12 mo and <4 nodules ≤3 cm**. Pts with prior adjuvant TAM were excluded.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Every pt had radical excision, then **5000 cGy at 200 cGy/fx**, 5 days a week, to the involved region. RT was fixed across arms, so the trial tests systemic therapy added to full local therapy.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: **Tamoxifen 20 mg/d** orally until progression vs observation.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: DFS favored TAM (log-rank **P=0.053**, Gehan-Wilcoxon **P=0.008**), with **no OS difference** (P=0.79). The benefit was confined to **postmenopausal pts (5-yr DFS 61% vs 33%, P=0.006)**. In the multivariate model, TAM and DFI >12 mo predicted longer DFS.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: No deaths from pulmonary embolism or endometrial cancer attributable to TAM in either menopausal group.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The authors describe this as the only randomized trial of systemic therapy for ILRR to reach its accrual goal. IBCSG Trial 27 was opened to test chemotherapy vs local treatment alone in LRR, a question this trial does not address.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents TAM-naive women with ER+ or small-volume, late post-mastectomy ILRR treated with excision and RT. Does not represent pts already given adjuvant endocrine therapy, recurrence after breast-conserving therapy, or poor-risk ILRR.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The early-weighted test carries the DFS result while log-rank misses 0.05. The menopausal split rests on small subgroups. Receptor status was not determined in about a third of pts.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The DFS benefit has persisted since the first analysis, but OS is unchanged, possibly because there were few events and competing mortality in postmenopausal pts. The premenopausal OS deficit with TAM is unexplained and nonsignificant, so it reads as noise more than harm.

studies.interpretation:
The trial's lasting value is less the tamoxifen result than what it shows about the natural history of isolated locoregional recurrence after mastectomy. The older view, set out in the paper's introduction, is that ILRR is mainly a marker of disseminated disease and that local treatment is palliative. Here, roughly 30% of good-risk pts in the observation arm stayed free of further local and distant relapse after excision and 5000 cGy, and close to 40% of the TAM arm had long-term disease control. That supports treating good-risk ILRR with curative intent and full-dose local therapy, rather than minimal surgery followed by systemic treatment alone.

For an RT reader, the pattern of failure is the informative part. In the authors' analysis, tamoxifen mainly reduced further local recurrence, and its effect on distant failure was not significant. So even after radical excision and 5000 cGy at 200 cGy/fx, a meaningful share of pts failed again in the field or nearby, and endocrine therapy acted largely as a local-control adjunct. This raises the question of whether that RT dose and target volume were enough, but the trial cannot answer it: RT was the same in both arms and the paper does not describe field design. Pairing the late distant-metastasis peak reported by Fortin et al. with the idea that ILRR can itself seed metastases strengthens the argument for eradicating the recurrence early and completely.

How much confidence the DFS result deserves depends on the statistics. The log-rank P was 0.053, and the stronger Gehan-Wilcoxon P of 0.008 gives more weight to early events. In practice, TAM delays relapse in the first years after ILRR, and the curves are less clearly separated later. That fits a disease-control effect better than a cure effect, and it agrees with the absent OS difference. The authors attribute the null OS to small numbers and competing non-cancer deaths in older pts. That is plausible but cannot be tested in a trial of this size.

The menopausal split should be read cautiously in both directions. The postmenopausal DFS gain (61% vs 33%, P=0.006) is large, but only about 35 premenopausal pts were enrolled. The premenopausal pattern of equal DFS and a numerically worse OS on TAM rests on very few events, and the authors' trophic-estrogen hypothesis is speculative. It is not a reason to withhold endocrine therapy from a premenopausal woman with ER+ ILRR.

The main limit on applying this today is the eligibility rule excluding prior adjuvant TAM. Most current pts with ER+ ILRR recur on or after adjuvant endocrine therapy, so the relevant question is a switch, for example to an aromatase inhibitor, which this trial did not test. The authors point to metastatic-setting data that aromatase inhibitors keep activity after TAM, but that is indirect. For poor-risk ILRR, the chemotherapy question went to IBCSG Trial 27. What would make this result wrong is if it does not transfer to receptor-defined modern pts: about a third of this cohort entered with receptor status undetermined, on volume and interval criteria alone.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Even after excision plus 5000 cGy at 200 cGy/fx, further local recurrence was the dominant failure, and TAM mainly reduced it. The trial supports full-dose curative-intent RT for good-risk ILRR combined with endocrine therapy as a local-control partner, not a replacement.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: The DFS gain from TAM was confined to postmenopausal women (5-yr 61% vs 33%, P=0.006) and did not translate into OS. Because pts with prior adjuvant TAM were excluded, the trial does not say which agent to use for today's endocrine-pretreated ER+ ILRR.

open_questions: Aromatase inhibitor benefit after ILRR in tamoxifen-pretreated pts
Role of chemotherapy for poor-risk ILRR
Optimal RT dose and volume after ILRR excision

studies.name: Node-negative post-mastectomy LRR and prognostic factors
studies.tldr: 10y LRR 6.0% overall in N0 post-mastectomy pts without PMRT, rising to 40.6% with 3 risk factors (size >2 cm, margin <2 mm, premenopausal, LVI).
details: 🔍 Retrospective MGH cohort, 877 node-negative cases (870 pts), mastectomy + ALND, 1980-2000
🔍 No pts received PMRT; T4 excluded; median f/u 100 mo
🔍 Median age 64; median 15 nodes examined
💊 Systemic therapy in 276 cases; none in 601
📊 10y cumulative incidence: total LRR 6.0%, isolated LRR 4.3%

details.text: 📊 10y total LRR by number of independent risk factors (p<0.0001)

details: 📐 MVA (Cox, stepwise): size, margin, LVI, menopausal status independent; HRs 2.6 to 3.8, similar in magnitude
⚠️ Grade associated on univariate only; dropped from MVA
⚠️ Systemic therapy subgroups: chemo + hormones 12.6% vs none 6.5% (p=0.04); selection bias per authors
⚠️ LVI not recorded pooled with LVI absent; possible misclassification
⚠️ Pre-modern systemic therapy era; receptor/HER2 status not reported in source
🔗 IBCSG analysis (1,275 N0 women) also found size, LVI, menopausal status predictive; margins not assessable there

verdict.rationale: Retrospective single-institution 1980-2000 cohort with no PMRT arm; stepwise risk model unvalidated, high-risk strata small with wide SEs. Defines who might benefit, not benefit itself.
verdict.audience: Node-negative breast, T1-3, mastectomy + ALND, no PMRT

studies.significance: Chest wall was the failure site in 80.4% of total LRRs, which is the basis for the authors' chest wall-only field proposal in high-risk N0. The 3-factor stratum (10y LRR 40.6% ± 13.8%) sits near the node-positive LRR range where PMRT gained survival, but its wide error makes it a threshold argument, not an indication.
studies.monday_clinic: In node-negative pts after mastectomy with T2+ tumor, deep margin <2 mm and LVI (or premenopausal with any 2 of these), this supports discussing chest wall PMRT; it does not extend to N0 pts with 0 or 1 factors (10y LRR 1.2% and 10.0%).

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Retrospective** single-institution cohort (Massachusetts General Hospital), 1980-2000, identified via tumor registry and breast center databases. **Median f/u 100 mo.** LRR estimated by cumulative incidence (CIF); KM results reported as slightly higher, not substantially different.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **877 node-negative invasive cases** (870 pts) after mastectomy + axillary dissection, **no PMRT**; T4 excluded. Median age 64, median 15 nodes examined. Systemic therapy in 276 cases (148 hormones alone, 74 chemo alone, 54 both).

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Total LRR** (first event, with or without simultaneous distant mets) and isolated LRR (no distant mets for ≥4 mo). Only total LRR reported for prognostic factors.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: 10y total LRR **6.0%**. Size >2 cm, deep margin <2 mm, premenopausal status and LVI independent on MVA with similar HRs (range 2.6 to 3.8). **3 factors: 10y LRR 40.6%**; only 1 pt had all 4.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: No RT delivered. Chest wall was the site in **87.5% of isolated and 80.4% of total** failures, so the authors propose **chest wall-only PMRT without regional nodes** for high-risk N0 to limit toxicity.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Converges with the IBCSG analysis of 1,275 N0 women on size, LVI and menopausal status, and adds **margin status**, which IBCSG could not assess. The M. D. Anderson series (141 N0 pts) did not report absolute LRR for its N0 subset.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents T1-3 node-negative pts after mastectomy + ALND with no PMRT. Does not represent T4, sentinel-only staging, or pts on uniform modern systemic therapy.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Most cases (601/877) had **no systemic therapy**, so absolute risks likely overstate the modern setting. Receptor subtype not reported. LVI not recorded was pooled with absent, and the risk count assumes equal weights.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Authors suggest considering PMRT for **postmenopausal pts with all 3 of T2+, close/positive margin and LVI**, and **premenopausal pts with any 2**. Benefit of PMRT in these strata is inferred from risk level, never tested.

studies.interpretation:
The headline 6.0% 10-year LRR confirms why node-negative mastectomy pts have generally not received PMRT. The paper's value is the gradient underneath that average. Four factors (tumor >2 cm, deep margin <2 mm, premenopausal status, LVI) each held up on multivariate analysis with hazard ratios in a narrow band, and that similarity is what licenses the authors' simple additive count. Once three coexist, 10-year LRR reaches 40.6%, a level the authors place beside the node-positive and T3 populations in which randomized PMRT data showed a survival gain. That is the core argument: nodal status is a proxy for LRR risk, and where the proxy misleads, the risk itself should drive the PMRT conversation.

How much weight the upper strata can carry is the first question. The 3-factor estimate carries a standard error of ±13.8% and the 2-factor estimate ±7.5%, which tells you these groups are small. Only one pt had all four factors. The model was built by stepwise selection from univariate hits in a single cohort with no validation set, which tends to overstate how cleanly the factors separate risk. Grade showed a univariate gradient (0%, 5.3%, 10%) but dropped out, more plausibly from overlap with size or LVI than from irrelevance. The LVI coding, which pooled unrecorded with absent, was a defensible call given pathology practice of the era; misclassification of that kind would tend to dilute the LVI effect rather than inflate it.

The era matters more than any single analytic choice. Cases span 1980 to 2000, 601 of 877 received no systemic therapy, and receptor and HER2 status are not reported in the source. The authors themselves concede that modern systemic therapy may lower these absolute risks, and that the higher LRR with combined chemo and hormones (12.6%) reflects selection rather than harm. The 40.6% figure is best read as an upper bound from an untreated-era population. The strongest support for the factors being real is convergence: the IBCSG analysis of 1,275 node-negative women found size, LVI and menopausal status predictive, and this cohort adds deep margin status, which IBCSG could not test because positive margins were excluded from its trials.

For the RT decision, the chest wall-only field proposal rests on the pattern of failure: the chest wall accounted for 80.4% of total LRR, with only 5 supraclavicular failures. That inference assumes failure sites in an unirradiated cohort predict where PMRT benefit lies, and it rests on 46 total events. The paper would be wrong in practice if modern systemic therapy and receptor-guided treatment compress the high-risk tail so that no N0 stratum approaches the LRR level of the node-positive trials. It defines a hypothesis about who might benefit from PMRT; it does not show that PMRT helps node-negative pts, since none were irradiated.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Chest wall was the failure site in 80.4% of total LRRs, supporting chest wall-only fields over regional nodal coverage in high-risk N0. The 3-factor stratum (10y LRR 40.6% ± 13.8%) frames a risk threshold for discussing PMRT, not proof of benefit.

open_questions: Does chest wall-only PMRT reduce LRR in high-risk node-negative pts?
Do modern systemic therapy and receptor subtype lower these LRR estimates?
Can biomarkers refine LRR risk beyond clinicopathologic factors?

studies.name: NSABP B-15/B-16/B-18/B-22/B-25 IBTR and LRR prognosis
studies.tldr: After lumpectomy + WBI in node-positive pts, IBTR (HR 2.58) and other LRR (HR 5.85) predicted death; 5-yr OS 59.9% vs 24.1%.
details: 🔍 Pooled analysis of 2,669 lumpectomy pts from 5 NSABP node-positive adjuvant trials, median time on study 13.3 yrs
🔍 All had lumpectomy, whole-breast irradiation and adjuvant systemic therapy; negative margins required for eligibility
⚠️ WBI dose, fractionation and nodal field use not reported in source

details.text: 📊 Outcomes after IBTR vs other LRR (oLRR)

subdetails: Sites: 47 axillary, 81 supraclavicular, 13 chest wall, 7 scar only, 17 other/multiple
IBTR by pathologic size >4 cm vs ≤2 cm: 14.3% v 7.5% (P=.045)
IBTR lowest with ER >100 fmol or unknown: 4.5% (ER P=.0007)
IBTR not associated with nodal count (P=.53)
oLRR associated with ER-neg (P=.011) and PgR-neg (P=.0073)

details.text: 📊 10-yr cumulative IBTR and oLRR by protocol
📐 No between-protocol IBTR difference after age adjustment (P=.50)

details: 📊 Later IBTR: >40% reduction in 3-yr mortality risk vs earlier IBTR, across cutoffs
⚠️ Prognostic association only: cannot show that preventing LRR would avert the excess deaths
⚠️ 1984-1994 regimens; premenopausal pts got no tamoxifen regardless of ER status

verdict.rationale: Post-hoc pooled analysis of a non-randomized lumpectomy subset; LRR is a prognostic marker here, not a tested intervention target. Pre-taxane, pre-HER2 era therapy.
verdict.audience: Node-positive breast, lumpectomy + WBI + adjuvant chemo and/or tamoxifen

studies.significance: Supraclavicular failure is the RT-relevant read: it made up 81 of 165 oLRRs and carried 5-yr DDFS 12.1% vs 31.5% after axillary recurrence. oLRR reached 14.6% at 10 yrs with ≥10 positive nodes, so nodal burden frames the regional-field question after BCS; field design was not reported in source.
studies.monday_clinic: In a node-positive pt with an isolated in-breast or regional recurrence after lumpectomy and WBI, this supports treating the event as a marker of high distant risk when weighing restaging and systemic options; it does not describe recurrence risk under taxane or HER2-directed therapy.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Pooled secondary analysis** of 5 NSABP node-positive adjuvant trials (B-15, B-16, B-18, B-22, B-25). Cumulative incidence for IBTR and oLRR; IBTR and oLRR entered Cox models as **time-varying covariates**. Median time on study 13.3 yrs.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Of 10,010 women entered, **2,669** had breast-conserving surgery and were eligible. **Negative margins** were required; about two thirds had 1-3 positive nodes. B-18 contributed only its postoperative chemotherapy arm.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: AC, CMF, PF/PAF and tamoxifen-based adjuvant regimens from 1984-1994, including AC cyclophosphamide intensification in B-22 and B-25. Pts aged >50 received tamoxifen in several protocols; **premenopausal women did not receive tamoxifen** irrespective of ER status.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: All pts received **whole-breast irradiation** after lumpectomy. Dose, fractionation, boost and any regional nodal coverage are **not reported in source**.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: Cumulative incidence of IBTR and oLRR; DDFS and OS after each event; mortality modeled with clinical factors plus IBTR or oLRR.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: oLRR carried **roughly double the mortality hazard of IBTR** (HR 5.85 vs 2.58), and supraclavicular recurrence had the poorest DDFS. Arm-level values are in the detail table.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Consistent with the NSABP B-06 IBTR literature the authors cite and with the EBCTCG overview linking local failure to breast cancer mortality. The supraclavicular-dominant oLRR pattern is the population later addressed by randomized RNI trials such as MA.20 and EORTC 22922.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents node-positive pts after margin-negative lumpectomy with WBI and 1984-1994 era chemotherapy and/or tamoxifen. Does not represent node-negative disease, mastectomy pts, or taxane, HER2-directed or CDK4/6-era therapy.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Lumpectomy was not the randomized variable, so the 2,669-pt subset is self-selected. Site-specific DDFS estimates rest on small numbers with wide CIs, and no HER2 or RT technique data are available.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: oLRR clusters with nodal burden and receptor negativity, the same drivers of distant failure, so it may flag disseminated disease rather than cause it. Later IBTRs fared better, consistent with the authors' view that many are new primaries. The role of chemotherapy at recurrence was **unresolved** at publication.

studies.interpretation:
The headline association, that locoregional failure after breast-conserving therapy marks a worse outcome, is not new; the authors place it alongside the NSABP B-06 recurrence analyses, and the EBCTCG overview cited here argued that local control and breast cancer mortality are linked. What this pooled cohort adds is the node-positive, chemotherapy-treated setting and a clean separation of in-breast failure from regional and other locoregional failure. Those two behave as different diseases. An IBTR roughly doubles the mortality hazard (HR 2.58), while an oLRR carries an HR of 5.85, and the gap in 5-yr OS after the event (59.9% vs 24.1%) is too wide to read as one phenomenon.

Methodologically, modeling recurrence as a time-varying covariate is the right choice. It avoids crediting the recurrence-free group with the survival time pts needed simply to be at risk of recurring, a bias that inflated older landmark-free comparisons. Cumulative incidence with competing risks is also appropriate. But the design answers a prognostic question, not a causal one. oLRR clusters with nodal burden and ER and PgR negativity, the same features that drive distant failure, so the recurrence may be the first visible sign of disseminated disease rather than a source of it. Nothing here apportions how much of the excess mortality preventing the recurrence would avert, and a reader should not take the HRs as the survival gain available from better local therapy. The timing data support the same caution from the other direction: later IBTRs carried more than a 40% reduction in 3-yr mortality risk versus earlier ones, consistent with the authors' suggestion that many late in-breast events are new primaries rather than persistent disease.

For a radiation oncologist the most useful signal sits in the oLRR breakdown. Supraclavicular recurrences were the largest group, 81 of 165, and had the poorest course, 5-yr DDFS 12.1% against 31.5% after axillary recurrence, while oLRR incidence at 10 yrs rose from 4.4% with 1-3 nodes to 14.6% with ≥10. The source describes whole-breast irradiation only and gives no field, dose or nodal-coverage detail, so these cannot be classed as in-field or marginal failures. The dataset identifies the at-risk population; whether regional nodal irradiation changes its course was the question MA.20 and EORTC 22922 later took up with randomization, and this analysis cannot substitute for them.

Transferability is the main limit. These are 1984-1994 regimens: no taxanes, no HER2 testing or HER2-directed therapy, and premenopausal ER-positive women went without tamoxifen. Lumpectomy was not randomized, so the 2,669-pt subset reflects surgeon and pt selection. Margin-negative status was mandatory, which removes margin as an explanatory variable. Absolute locoregional failure rates and post-recurrence survival are both likely different with modern systemic therapy and salvage options. The paper leaves the treatment of an isolated recurrence explicitly open, noting a then-new IBCSG and NSABP trial of chemotherapy at relapse. Read it as a durable description of who fails locoregionally and how badly, not as a measure of what local therapy buys.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Supraclavicular failure dominated oLRR (81 of 165) and had 5-yr DDFS 12.1%, while oLRR hit 14.6% at 10 yrs with ≥10 nodes. This frames the regional-field question after BCS in node-positive disease, though WBI technique and nodal coverage were not reported in source.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: An oLRR carried mortality HR 5.85 and an IBTR 2.58, with 5-yr DDFS 18.8% and 51.4% after each, so a locoregional relapse signals high distant risk. Whether chemotherapy at relapse helps was unresolved; regimens predate taxanes and HER2-directed therapy.

open_questions: Does regional nodal RT reduce supraclavicular failure in this population?
Does chemotherapy at isolated locoregional recurrence improve survival?
Can molecular profiling separate true IBTR from new ipsilateral primaries?

studies.name: T1-2N1 mastectomy without PMRT (MSKCC)
studies.tldr: 10y LRR 7.0% without PMRT vs 4.0% with it (p=0.32) in T1-2N1 after mastectomy; age <40 + LVI reached 28% without PMRT.
details: 🔍 Single-institution retrospective, prospectively maintained MSKCC database, mastectomy 1995-2006
🔍 N=1087 T1-2N1: 924 (85%) no PMRT, 163 (15%) PMRT at physician discretion
🔍 Excluded T3/T4, neoadjuvant chemo, isolated tumor cells only
🔍 Median f/u 10.8 yr (range 0-21)

📊 LRR without PMRT by age and LVI (Fig 2)
📐 MVA for LRR in no-PMRT group

details.text: 📊 Pattern of failure, 63 LRRs total (7 PMRT, 56 no PMRT)

details: 🔍 PMRT: chest wall in all; SCV 137/163 (84%), axilla 7 (4%), IMN 6 (4%). Dose/fractionation not reported
🔍 ALND in 94.2%, median 18 nodes resected; chemo 88%, anthracycline and/or taxane 76%
⚠️ PMRT group enriched for younger age, larger T, LVI, ECE, more +LNs: selection makes the arm comparison uninterpretable
⚠️ HER2-amplified: only 51/123 (41%) received trastuzumab

verdict.rationale: Retrospective, non-randomized; PMRT selected for higher-risk pts, so null LRR/RFS/OS difference cannot estimate PMRT effect. Risk-stratification value lies in the no-PMRT cohort only.
verdict.audience: T1-2N1 breast, mastectomy + ALND, no neoadjuvant chemo

studies.significance: The RT read is the no-PMRT stratification: 10y LRR 28% for age <40 with LVI vs 2% for ≥40 without LVI. Supraclavicular nodes carried 27% of LRRs and the axilla only 15.9%, so where PMRT is chosen for the high-risk stratum, the regional field targets where these pts actually failed.
studies.monday_clinic: In a woman ≥40 with T1-2N1, no LVI, after mastectomy with completion ALND and no neoadjuvant chemo, this supports omitting PMRT; it does not extend to a positive-sentinel axilla left undissected or to post-NAC pts.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Single-institution **retrospective** cohort from a prospectively maintained database, mastectomy 1995-2006. PMRT given at physician discretion. Median follow-up **10.8 yr**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **T1-2N1** (1-3 positive nodes), N=1087. Excluded T3/T4, **neoadjuvant chemotherapy**, and isolated tumor cells. Median age 51, median tumor 1.8 cm; 58% had one positive node.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: All PMRT pts received **chest wall** RT; supraclavicular field in 137/163 (84%), axilla 7 (4%), IMN 6 (4%). Dose and fractionation not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Systemic therapy in 98%; chemo 88%, mostly anthracycline and/or taxane. All ER+ pts received hormone therapy; trastuzumab in 51/123 HER2-amplified.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Without PMRT, **age <40** (HR 4.15) and **LVI** (HR 3.47) independently predicted LRR. Chest wall (51%) and supraclavicular nodes (27%) dominated failure sites.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The EBCTCG 1-3 node subset showed **20.3%** 10-yr LRR without PMRT, versus **7.0%** here, a gap the authors attribute to modern systemic therapy and thorough ALND (median 18 nodes). EORTC 22922 included lumpectomy and stage I-III pts, limiting direct comparison.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents T1-2N1 pts after mastectomy with completion ALND and adjuvant systemic therapy. Does not represent pts with positive sentinel nodes without completion ALND, or pts treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Dose and target-volume data absent, so the 4.0% PMRT LRR cannot be tied to a technique. Pathology not re-reviewed, and HER2-directed therapy was incomplete in the cohort. The 10-yr LRR 28% subgroup CI as printed (11.0-22.1) excludes its own estimate.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The useful product is a **risk filter for omission**, not a PMRT efficacy estimate. It shows age and LVI separating a 2% from a 28% 10-yr LRR in unirradiated pts, which is the decision a T1-2N1 consult turns on.

studies.interpretation:
This paper is best read as a natural history of selectively unirradiated T1-2N1 disease, not as a test of PMRT. The headline comparison, 10-year LRR 4.0% with PMRT versus 7.0% without and overlapping RFS and OS curves, is the least informative part of the analysis. The 163 irradiated women were chosen precisely because they looked worse: younger, larger tumors, more LVI, more extracapsular extension, more positive nodes. A null unadjusted difference between a high-risk treated group and a low-risk untreated group says only that clinicians at this center triaged sensibly, which the authors themselves acknowledge when they warn against reading Fig 1 as a randomized comparison.

The value lies in the 924 women who did not get PMRT. Their 7.0% 10-year LRR sits far below the 20.3% the EBCTCG reported for the 1-3 node subset, and in line with the 4-10% the authors cite from contemporary series. That gap is the central argument for de-escalation in this population: the absolute LRR benefit PMRT can deliver shrinks as the baseline risk falls, and the EBCTCG mortality benefit was estimated against a baseline that no longer describes most pts. The plausible explanations offered, anthracycline/taxane chemotherapy, aromatase inhibitors, and an ALND removing a median of 18 nodes, are reasonable but untested here, and the cohort was treated before trastuzumab was universal, so a modern HER2+ population would likely sit lower still.

The stratification by age and LVI is where a radiation oncologist should spend attention. A 10-year LRR of 2% in women 40 and older without LVI is a level at which PMRT toxicity, cardiac dose and reconstruction complications plausibly outweigh benefit. A 28% rate in women under 40 with LVI is in the range where historical trials showed a survival gain, and the authors agree it warrants PMRT. The two intermediate cells (11% and 8%) are where the decision remains genuinely open, and this dataset cannot resolve them. Confidence in the extreme cells should also be tempered: the high-risk subgroup started with only 75 women, and the printed confidence interval for the 28% estimate does not contain the point estimate, suggesting a reporting error.

The pattern of failure matters for anyone who does irradiate. Chest wall carried half the recurrences and supraclavicular nodes about a quarter, while the dissected axilla contributed little. This supports chest wall plus supraclavicular coverage when PMRT is chosen, and argues that the axillary field adds little after a thorough dissection. It also cuts the other way for the modern axilla: these outcomes rest on 94% ALND, and the authors explicitly say omission does not transfer to pts with positive sentinel nodes who skip completion dissection. In the post-AMAROS era, where many such pts receive nodal RT in place of ALND, this cohort's low regional recurrence cannot be borrowed to justify omitting both.

For this to mislead, unmeasured selection within the no-PMRT group would need to have kept high-risk features out of it beyond what age and LVI capture, which is plausible given discretionary allocation. Randomized evidence on intermediate-risk PMRT, such as SUPREMO, is the appropriate check on whether these thresholds hold.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Without PMRT, 10y LRR spans 2% (≥40, no LVI) to 28% (<40, LVI), defining whom to offer RT. Supraclavicular nodes carried 27% of LRRs versus 15.9% axillary involvement, supporting chest wall plus SCV coverage when PMRT is chosen.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: The low LRR without PMRT rests on ALND in 94.2% with a median 18 nodes removed; the authors state omission does not apply to positive sentinel nodes without completion ALND. For women <40 with LVI, they suggest axillary RT may replace completion ALND.

open_questions: Does age/LVI risk stratification hold after SLNB without completion ALND?
Should intermediate-risk T1-2N1 pts (one of age <40 or LVI) receive PMRT?
Does modern HER2-directed therapy lower LRR further without PMRT?

papers.title: Adjuvant therapy after excision and radiation of isolated postmastectomy locoregional breast cancer recurrence: definitive results of a phase III randomized trial (SAKK 23/82) comparing tamoxifen with observation
Prognosis After Ipsilateral Breast Tumor Recurrence and Locoregional Recurrences in Five National Surgical Adjuvant Breast and Bowel Project Node-Positive Adjuvant Breast Cancer Trials
papers.abstract: Purpose Locoregional failure after breast-conserving surgery is associated with increased risk of distant disease and death. The magnitude of this risk in patients receiving chemotherapy has not been adequately characterized. Patients and Methods Our study population included 2,669 women randomly assigned onto five National Surgical Adjuvant Breast and Bowel Project node-positive protocols (B-15, B-16, B-18, B-22, and B-25), who were treated with lumpectomy, whole-breast irradiation, and adjuvant systemic therapy. Cumulative incidences of ipsilateral breast tumor recurrence (IBTR) and other locoregional recurrence (oLRR) were calculated. Kaplan-Meier curves were used to estimate distant–disease-free survival (DDFS) and overall survival (OS) after IBTR or oLRR. Cox models were used to model survival using clinical and pathologic factors jointly with IBTR or oLRR as time-varying predictors. Results Four hundred twenty-four patients (15.9%) experienced locoregional failure; 259 (9.7%) experienced IBTR, and 165 (6.2%) experienced oLRR. The 10-year cumulative incidence of IBTR and oLRR was 8.7% and 6.0%, respectively. Most locoregional failures occurred within 5 years (62.2% for IBTR and 80.6% for oLRR). Age, tumor size, and estrogen receptor status were significantly associated with IBTR. Nodal status and estrogen and progesterone receptor status were significantly associated with oLRR. The 5-year DDFS rates after IBTR and oLRR were 51.4% and 18.8%, respectively. The 5-year OS rates after IBTR and oLRR were 59.9% and 24.1%, respectively. Hazard ratios for mortality associated with IBTR and oLRR were 2.58 (95% CI, 2.11 to 3.15) and 5.85 (95% CI, 4.80 to 7.13), respectively. Conclusion Node-positive breast cancer patients who developed IBTR or oLRR had significantly poorer prognoses than patients who did not experience these events.
